newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer sees no shift from steady rate policy.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer sees no shift from steady rate policy.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Sunday he saw no reason for the German central bank to deviate from its steady hand policy on interest rates.
"Steady hand monetary policy is something that I believe has paid off, which is correct, which is necessary," he said in an interview with German radio, a text of which was released in advance.
"And at the moment I see no reason to change this monetary policy," Tietmeyer added.
Tietmeyer also said that Germany was in a happy position of having an inflation rate well below two percent and hoped to keep it below that level in the longer term.

The Bundesbank has kept its headline Lombard and discount rates on hold since April 1996, when it eased them to 4.50 percent and 2.50 percent respectively. The money market rate, or repo, has been at three percent since August.
Tietmeyer said also that French monetary policy was running on a stable course and he saw no risk to the franc-deutschemark exchange rate from the new government.
Tietmeyer said France was aware of the importance of stable exchange rates with other European countries.
"I believe that French monetary policy is on a very stable course and I assume that the franc-mark relationship is not up for discussion," Tietmeyer said.

Noting that the franc-mark relation had been relatively stable of late, Tietmeyer said: "If I have understood the politics correctly, the new government will do what it can not to put this result at risk."
Tietmeyer denied the Bundesbank had declared patronage for the French franc in the past, but he said it had helped the franc to win market trust in the past.
"And I see no reason why this should not be also so in the future. Declarations of patronage are not necessary," he said.
Tietmeyer noted job creation schemes being mooted in France ran counter to previous policies but said policies were still at an early stage and had not translated into concrete budget strategies.
"We must wait and see. But I am convinced that people in France see very clearly how important a stable exchange rate between the French franc and the other European currencies is."
